newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican demand revisions cast doubt over 97 GDP.
newsitem.headline: Mexican demand revisions cast doubt over 97 GDP.

text.p: On the basis of unexpectedly-weak 1996 private consumption data, some Mexican economists believe the government may be over-estimating economic growth in 1997.

Last week, the National Statistics Institute (INEGI) issued its breakdown of aggregate supply and demand last year, and it drastically revised down private demand figures that make up an important chunk of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
The revisions irritated economists, some of whom had battled with INEGI last year because they believed its estimates of private demand were exaggerated.

But for those who were bearish on the much-vaunted consumer recovery, the numbers bore out what they had long been saying and hearing anecdotally -- that Mexicans do not feel like they have bounced back from crisis.
"Even though there is a recovery, frankly it cannot be that big. Private consumption does not have the force that people thought it had," Sergio Martin, economist at ING Barings, said.
He said the murky picture of overall consumption -- that accounts for almost 70 percent of GDP -- reinforced his view that the economy would grow just 4 percent this year.
The government, hailing a rebound in private demand, has predicted 4.5 percent growth for 1997.
According to the latest INEGI data, private demand grew by 2.3 percent in 1996, part of a 5.1 percent GDP growth rate.

Quarterly, INEGI revised the changes in private demand as follows: Q1, -0.5 percent; Q2, 2.4 percent; Q3, 3.0 percent. Previously it had reported Q1 growth of 1.3 percent, Q2 growth of 2.9 percent and Q3 growth of 5.5 percent. It reported Q4 growth of 4.4 percent.
The revisions raised eyebrows, even anger among investors. But the third quarter number particularly stunned economists.
"That's all the difference in the world, you're talking about nearly cutting your number in half," Gray Newman, economist at HSBC James Capel, said.
He said he had doubted INEGI's portrayal of such a strong consumer revival last year. The revisions told a new story.

"It really represents an about face on the part of the authorities regarding the nature of consumer spending," he said. "It's quite important because it's based on these numbers that you estimate 1997 GDP growth."
Newman is forecasting GDP growth as low as 3.5 percent this year, at the bottom end of the spectrum, and he said he was unlikely to revise that upward.
The demand data "is probably going to confirm our numbers and cause some people to revise them downward," he said.
Economists say private demand continues to be stunted by high family debt levels, and a continued drop in real wages. The

numbers tally with retail sales data also released by INEGI that were weak all last year. Supermarket and department store sales have also continued to slump, though analysts say the rate of decline is falling.

Denis Parisien of Bankers Trust in New York said he was sticking to a 4.8 percent growth projection for 1997, but he aired concerns about the revisions and wondered how secure the 4.4 percent Q4 private demand growth rate was.
"The constant revisions raise doubts among analysts as to whether or not the surprising Q4 1996 increase will stand the test of time," he said.
